newsitem.title: USA: Mass. mutual insurers seek liberalized rules.
newsitem.headline: Mass. mutual insurers seek liberalized rules.

text.p: Massachusetts-based mutual insurance companies on Wednesday threw their weight behind a bill that would allow them to issue stock to raise capital.
The bill, S. 657, would allow the creation of so-called hybrid mutuals, allowing them to convert into mutual holding companies.
Under present rules, mutuals -- which are owned by their policyholders -- cannot access capital markets, because they cannot issue stock.
Among the companies pushing for the legislation are John Hancock Mutual Life Insurance Co., Massachusetts Mutual Life Insurance Co., and Berkshire Life Insurance Co.
So far, about 10 U.S. states have approved these hybrid companies, and Massachusetts and New York are among the dozen other states debating it, industry analysts said.
The Center for Insurance Research (CIR), a Cambridge, Mass.-based consumer group, is adamantly opposed to the bill.
CIR Executive Director Jason Adkins told Reuters that the law could be "a disaster" for policyholders.
He said that mutual companies have no right to take away money that rightfully belongs to policyholders, who are entitled to the company's assets when it is converted and sold.
But mutual insurers told a legislative committee hearing on Wednesday that the new measures are needed to keep them competitive against out of state rivals and publically traded companies.

"Competition with banks, mutual fund companies and stock insurers is fierce and requires access to capital," Tracy Rich, deputy general counsel of Massachusetts Mutual Life Insurance Co., testified before the Joint Committee on Insurance.
"As an industry, we need the flexibility to change with the times," he said.
Under the bill, a company that wants to reorganize would convert into a stock insurance company that issues the policies, and a mutual holding company that owns the stock insurance company.
The stock insurance company would be able to sell stock, while the mutual holding company would retain a controlling interest in the stock insurer.
"Right now, our only option is to demutualize," said David Kalib, general counsel of the Pittsfield, Mass.-based Berkshire Life Insurance Company.

Kalib said demutualization was not a good option, "because it would leave us exposed to takeover by another company, threatening our existence in western Massachusetts and the jobs we provide to the area."
